issue.title: feat(tts): add VoxCPM2 engine support (Apache-2.0, 48kHz, 30 languages incl. Arabic)
issue.body:
## Summary

Add **VoxCPM2** (OpenBMB) as a first-class TTS engine in Voicebox, alongside the existing Qwen / Chatterbox / TADA / Kokoro / LuxTTS / F5-TTS backends.

VoxCPM2 is a 2B-parameter, Apache-2.0, 48 kHz TTS model supporting **30 languages including Arabic**, with zero-shot voice cloning, transcript-aligned "ultimate" cloning, and text-prompted voice *design*. Its Python API maps almost one-to-one onto our existing `TTSBackend` protocol, so this is an additive integration rather than an architectural change.

---

## Resources

| What | URL |
|---|---|
| Demo page / samples | https://openbmb.github.io/voxcpm2-demopage/ |
| Source repository | https://github.com/OpenBMB/VoxCPM |
| Model weights (HF) | https://huggingface.co/openbmb/VoxCPM2 |
| PyPI package | https://pypi.org/project/voxcpm/ |
| Our backend protocol | [`backend/backends/__init__.py#L68`](https://github.com/samykabu/voicebox/blob/main/backend/backends/__init__.py#L68) |
| Reference implementation to copy | [`backend/backends/luxtts_backend.py`](https://github.com/samykabu/voicebox/blob/main/backend/backends/luxtts_backend.py) |

---

## The problem we want to fix

Our current engine line-up leaves three real gaps:

1. **Arabic depends on a non-commercial checkpoint.** Our best broad-dialect Arabic option is `habibi-unified`, which is `CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0` (`commercial_use=False`). The commercially-safe alternative, `habibi-msa`, is MSA-only. VoxCPM2 is **Apache-2.0** and covers Arabic, giving us an unrestricted Arabic path for the first time.

2. **No single engine covers both wide multilingual reach and high-fidelity cloning.** Chatterbox covers 23 languages but needs output trimming (`needs_trim=True`). Kokoro is fast but has no cloning at all. LuxTTS is 48 kHz but English-focused. VoxCPM2 is 48 kHz, 30 languages, *and* clones.

3. **We have no voice *design* capability.** Every engine today requires a reference audio sample to produce a custom voice. VoxCPM2 can synthesize a voice from a plain-text description — `"(A young woman, gentle and sweet)Hello!"` — which unlocks voice creation for users who have no recording to clone from.

---

## Features we need to support

### Must have (v1)

- [ ] **New engine `voxcpm`** registered in `TTS_ENGINES`, selectable in the UI exactly like every other engine.
- [ ] **Standard TTS** — `generate(text, ...)` returning `(np.ndarray, 48000)`.
- [ ] **Zero-shot voice cloning** from an existing Voice Profile's reference audio (`prompt_wav_path` + `prompt_text`).
- [ ] **Voice prompt caching** via `get_cache_key` / `cache_voice_prompt`, matching the LuxTTS and F5 backends.
- [ ] **Multi-sample profiles** — implement `combine_voice_prompts` so profiles with several reference clips work.
- [ ] **Seeded / reproducible generation** — honour the `seed` argument through `manual_seed`.
- [ ] **Model download progress** — wrap loading in `model_load_progress(...)` so the Model Management UI shows the download bar.
- [ ] **Load / unload lifecycle** — `unload_model()` must free VRAM via `empty_device_cache`.
- [ ] **Language list** — register supported languages so the language picker filters correctly, with **Arabic explicitly verified end-to-end**.
- [ ] **Graceful unavailability** — VoxCPM2 is CUDA-only (see risks). The engine must be hidden or clearly disabled on machines that cannot run it, rather than failing at generation time.

### Should have

- [ ] **Voice design from text** — expose the `(description)text` prefix through the existing `instruct` field so users can create a voice with no reference audio.
- [ ] **Generation tuning** — map `cfg_value` and `inference_timesteps` to sensible defaults; consider exposing them as advanced settings.
- [ ] **Arabic pronunciation dictionary compatibility** — confirm our diacritics/prefix matching from [PR #11](https://github.com/samykabu/voicebox/pull/11) applies cleanly to VoxCPM2 input text.
- [ ] **Docs** — add VoxCPM2 to [`docs/content/docs/developer/tts-engines.mdx`](https://github.com/samykabu/voicebox/blob/main/docs/content/docs/developer/tts-engines.mdx) and the model-management page.
- [ ] **E2E test** — add a case to `backend/tests/test_all_models_e2e.py`.

### Out of scope for v1

- Streaming synthesis (`generate_streaming`) — our pipeline is chunk-based today; track separately.
- VoxCPM 1.5 / 0.5B variants — ship **VoxCPM2 only**, as a single size. Adding variants pulls in the multi-size plumbing (`engine_has_model_sizes`, the `("qwen", "tada", "f5_tts")` special-case tuples) for no user benefit.
- The optional denoiser (`load_denoiser=True`).

---

## Proposed implementation

The API maps directly onto our protocol:

| `TTSBackend` protocol | VoxCPM2 |
|---|---|
| `load_model()` | `VoxCPM.from_pretrained("openbmb/VoxCPM2", load_denoiser=False)` |
| `generate(text, voice_prompt, seed)` | `model.generate(text=..., prompt_wav_path=..., prompt_text=..., cfg_value=..., inference_timesteps=..., seed=...)` |
| `instruct` | voice design via `(description)` text prefix |
| returns `(audio, sample_rate)` | wav @ `model.tts_model.sample_rate` = 48 kHz |

### Files to touch

**New**
- `backend/backends/voxcpm_backend.py` — ~200 lines, modelled on `luxtts_backend.py`.

**Backend registry** — `backend/backends/__init__.py`
- `TTS_ENGINES` (L214) — add `"voxcpm": "VoxCPM2"`.
- `_get_non_qwen_tts_configs()` (L296) — add the `ModelConfig` (`license_id="Apache-2.0"`, `commercial_use=True`, `size_mb` ≈ 5000, full language list).
- `get_tts_backend_for_engine()` (L798) — add the dispatch branch.

**Validation & services**
- `backend/models.py` — four engine regex patterns at L92, L413, L432, L451.
- `backend/services/profiles.py` L27 — add `voxcpm` to `CLONING_ENGINES`.

**Install & packaging**
- `backend/requirements.txt` — VoxCPM sub-dependencies.
- `justfile` L67-74 (Unix) **and** L120-123 (Windows) — `pip install --no-deps voxcpm`, following the established pattern for chatterbox / hume-tada / f5-tts.
- `backend/build_binary.py` — hidden imports + data collection, mirroring the `kokoro` (L276) and `f5_tts` (L308) entries.

**Frontend** — `app/src`
- `lib/api/types.ts` L84 — engine union.
- `lib/constants/languages.ts` L73 — per-engine language map.
- `components/Generation/EngineModelSelector.tsx`, `components/Generation/FloatingGenerateBox.tsx`, `components/VoiceProfiles/ProfileForm.tsx`, `lib/hooks/useGenerationForm.ts`, `lib/utils/format.ts`, `components/ServerSettings/ModelManagement.tsx`.

---

## Risks & open questions

These need a dependency probe in a scratch venv **before** the backend is written.

1. **CUDA-only.** Upstream states CUDA >= 12.0 and documents no CPU or MPS path. This would be our first engine with **no macOS support at all**, and no CPU fallback. Needs a decision on how the UI presents an engine unavailable on the user's hardware. *Open question: does `voxcpm` actually run on CPU, just slowly?*

2. **Python version ceiling.** `voxcpm` requires Python `<3.13`. Our `requires-python` is `>=3.12` and the justfile falls back to 3.13 when 3.12 is absent — that fallback path would break.

3. **Dependency conflicts.** We pin `numpy<2.0` and `transformers<=4.57.6`. VoxCPM will almost certainly conflict, hence the `--no-deps` install. The full transitive dependency set needs to be enumerated by hand.

4. **Footprint.** ~8 GB VRAM and a multi-GB download — our heaviest engine. Confirm the actual `size_mb` for the Model Management UI.

5. **Frozen build size.** Adding another multi-GB model path affects the PyInstaller bundle; verify the desktop build still produces.

## Fork maintenance note

This is a fork-local feature. Keep the change **additive** — a new backend file plus registry entries — to minimise merge conflicts when syncing from `jamiepine/voicebox` upstream.

---

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] VoxCPM2 appears in the engine picker, downloads with a visible progress bar, and generates 48 kHz audio.
- [ ] A Voice Profile cloned with VoxCPM2 produces recognisable speaker likeness.
- [ ] Arabic generation works and respects the pronunciation dictionary.
- [ ] Model unload returns VRAM to the OS.
- [ ] `just setup` succeeds cleanly on Windows and Linux with the new dependency.
- [ ] The engine degrades gracefully (hidden or disabled with a clear reason) on unsupported hardware.
- [ ] Docs and the E2E test are updated.

<!-- speckit-scope:start -->
## Scope analysis

Effort: **13**

Each of cloning, caching, multi-sample combining, seeding, download progress, unload, language registration and graceful unavailability is independently testable, which is what makes this broad rather than merely long. integration=3: a multi-GB external model installed --no-deps against two hard pins (numpy<2.0, transformers<=4.57.6) whose transitive set is not yet enumerated; a Python <3.13 ceiling against a justfile fallback to 3.13; a PyInstaller frozen bundle that must still produce; and a cross-component contract gap, since no route exposes TTS_ENGINES and the frontend hardcodes its own engine and language lists, so Principle III's declared-capabilities requirement has no existing mechanism to use. Principle V then pulls in the generated TypeScript client and backend/README.md if an endpoint appears. No unmerged prerequisites, but the internal contract work is real. data_security=0: no data migration, no tenancy, no authorization change and no new sensitive data path. Voice data handling is unchanged because the engine reuses the existing profile and cache plumbing, and the licensing change moves from CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 toward Apache-2.0, which loosens a restriction rather than creating exposure. Four material unknowns are open: whether voxcpm runs on CPU at all, the full transitive dependency list, the real size_mb for the Model Management UI, and how an engine unavailable on the user's hardware should be presented. The last is a design decision the issue explicitly leaves open. Sum 12 maps to 13 points. The score is above 5, which recommends considering decomposition; a four-way split along probe, capability-contract, backend, and frontend-with-docs seams was presented with its tradeoffs. The user reviewed that recommendation and chose to keep the issue whole as a single executable unit. The score is retained honestly at 13 rather than reduced to match that choice.

### Implementation alignment

No prerequisite issues exist; inspect reports ready=true with zero dependencies, zero sub-issues and zero comments. The delta is measured against main at the time of scoping. IMPLEMENTED TODAY: the TTSBackend protocol (backend/backends/__init__.py:68-135) already defines load_model, create_voice_prompt, combine_voice_prompts, generate, unload_model, is_loaded and _get_model_path, so a new engine is additive. LuxTTSBackend (backend/backends/luxtts_backend.py, 184 lines) is a complete working template for a single-size 48 kHz cloning engine and already uses every shared helper the issue names: model_load_progress, empty_device_cache, manual_seed, get_cache_key/cache_voice_prompt and the shared combine_voice_prompts in backends/base.py. ModelConfig already carries license_id, commercial_use, languages and size_mb, so the licensing metadata the issue wants has a home. The Arabic licensing gap the issue describes is confirmed: habibi-unified is CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 with commercial_use=False (backend/backends/__init__.py:391-401) and habibi-msa is Apache-2.0 but MSA-dialect only (:378-389); both ride engine=f5_tts rather than an engine of their own. - backend/backends/luxtts_backend.py:1-184 - the single-size 48 kHz cloning template to copy, including every shared helper named in the issue
- backend/backends/__init__.py:214-222 - TTS_ENGINES, 8 engines, no voxcpm
- backend/backends/__init__.py:296-311 - the ModelConfig list this engine joins
- backend/backends/__init__.py:798-861 - the dispatch chain and its Unknown-engine error derived from TTS_ENGINES
- backend/backends/__init__.py:378-401 - habibi-msa Apache-2.0 MSA-only versus habibi-unified CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 commercial_use=False: the confirmed Arabic licensing gap this engine closes
- backend/models.py:92,413,432,451 - the four identical engine regexes
- backend/services/profiles.py:27 - CLONING_ENGINES, voxcpm absent
- backend/requirements.txt:12,76 - transformers<=4.57.6 and numpy<2.0, the pins the --no-deps install protects
- justfile:21 - the python3.13 fallback that the voxcpm Python <3.13 ceiling puts at risk
- justfile:67-74,120-123 - the established --no-deps pattern on both platform paths
- backend/pyproject.toml:4 - requires-python >=3.12 is already compatible with the ceiling
- backend/routes/ - no route reads TTS_ENGINES; there is no server-to-client engine availability channel today
- app/src/components/Generation/EngineModelSelector.tsx:23-39 - hardcoded ENGINE_OPTIONS

WHY THIS MATTERS. Three gaps exist today. Second, no single engine currently offers both wide multilingual reach and high-fidelity cloning: Chatterbox reaches 23 languages but needs output trimming, Kokoro is fast but cannot clone at all, and LuxTTS is 48 kHz but English-focused. Upstream documents CUDA 12.0 or newer and no CPU or MPS path, which would make this the first engine in the product with no macOS support at all. What is the complete transitive dependency set, given that the install must use --no-deps to avoid breaking the existing numpy<2.0 and transformers<=4.57.6 pins? What is the real on-disk size, so the Model Management UI reports it honestly: roughly 8 GB of VRAM and a multi-GB download would make this the heaviest engine in the product. And does the Python upper bound of below 3.13 break the setup path? The project floor of Python 3.12 or newer is itself compatible with that ceiling; the actual risk is the setup script's fallback to Python 3.13 when 3.12 is absent.

```text
CONSTRAINTS LEARNED FROM THE EXISTING CODEBASE. The backend protocol every engine implements already covers loading, voice-prompt creation, multi-prompt combining, generation, unloading and load-state reporting, so this integration is additive rather than architectural. LuxTTS is the closest existing engine (single size, 48 kHz, cloning) and is the model to follow; it already uses the shared helpers for load progress, device cache clearing, seeding, prompt caching and multi-sample combining, and the new engine should use the same ones rather than inventing parallel machinery. The --no-deps install pattern is established four times over and exists on both the Unix and the Windows setup paths, so both must be edited together. Engine capability, meaning which languages and which accelerators, must be declared once on the backend and queried by callers: the project constitution forbids expressing engine-specific behaviour as engine-name branching in route handlers or the frontend, and requires a new engine to declare its accelerator support and either degrade to CPU or report unavailability rather than crash. That matters here because no mechanism for this exists yet: nothing in the API layer exposes the engine registry, and the frontend keeps its own hardcoded engine and language lists. If this work adds or changes an API surface, the typed models, the generated client and the backend API documentation must all move in the same change, and the generated client must not be hand-edited. Heavy model libraries must be imported lazily inside functions so application startup does not slow down as engines are added.

SCOPE BOUNDARIES. Ship VoxCPM2 only, as a single model size: no VoxCPM 1.5 and no 0.5B variant, so none of the multi-size machinery is touched. No streaming synthesis; the pipeline is chunk-based today and streaming is tracked separately. No optional denoiser. No transcript-aligned ultimate cloning beyond ordinary zero-shot cloning. Do not migrate the seven existing engines onto any capability mechanism this work introduces: only the new engine needs to use it. Do not remove or replace the existing Arabic models; VoxCPM2 is added alongside them. Do not change the project's Python floor, which would require a constitutional amendment.

KEEP IT ADDITIVE. This repository is a fork that must stay cheaply mergeable with its upstream. Shape the change as a new backend file plus registration entries, and avoid refactors that would complicate future merges.

HOW IT WILL BE JUDGED. The engine appears in the picker, downloads with a visible progress bar and produces 48 kHz audio. A profile cloned with it sounds recognisably like the speaker. Arabic works and respects the pronunciation dictionary. Unloading returns VRAM. Setup succeeds cleanly on both Windows and Linux without disturbing the existing dependency pins, and the packaged desktop build still produces. The engine degrades gracefully on unsupported hardware. Documentation and the end-to-end test suite are updated. Because the Python test suite does not run in continuous integration, the author must run it locally before requesting review and say so in the pull request.

```

# Feature Specification: VoxCPM2 Text-to-Speech Engine

**Feature Branch**: `feature/001-voxcpm2-tts-engine`

**Created**: 2026-09-22

**Status**: Draft

**Input**: GitHub issue [samykabu/voicebox#13](https://github.com/samykabu/voicebox/issues/13) — scoped at effort 13, kept whole as a single executable issue by explicit user decision.

User description: "Add VoxCPM2 as a first-class TTS engine in Voicebox so that users get an Apache-2.0, 48 kHz, 30-language engine that can both clone a voice from a sample and design one from a written description."

## User Scenarios & Testing *(mandatory)*

### User Story 1 - Generate speech in a language the product could not serve freely before (Priority: P1)

A user who needs Arabic speech for something they intend to publish or sell opens Voicebox, picks the new VoxCPM2 engine, chooses Arabic, types their text, and gets high-quality audio. Today their only broad-dialect Arabic option carries a non-commercial licence, and the commercially safe alternative only speaks Modern Standard Arabic. With this engine they no longer have to choose between licence safety and dialect coverage.

**Why this priority**: This is the reason the feature exists. It removes a licensing dead end that no amount of tuning to the existing engines can fix, and it is the one outcome that is worthless if any other part ships without it.

**Independent Test**: Select VoxCPM2, generate in Arabic and in at least two other supported languages, and confirm the produced audio is intelligible and the engine is presented as permissively licensed. Delivers value on its own even with no cloning and no voice design.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** a machine that can run the engine, **When** the user opens the engine picker, **Then** VoxCPM2 appears as a selectable option alongside the existing engines.
2. **Given** VoxCPM2 is selected for the first time, **When** the user starts generation or triggers a download, **Then** a download progress indicator appears, reports advancing progress, and completes without the user having to guess whether anything is happening.
3. **Given** the engine is ready, **When** the user generates from text, **Then** speech is produced at the engine's full 48 kHz quality.
4. **Given** the user opens the language selector with VoxCPM2 chosen, **When** the list renders, **Then** exactly the languages this engine supports are offered, and Arabic is among them.
5. **Given** Arabic text containing words covered by the pronunciation dictionary, **When** generation runs, **Then** those words are pronounced as the dictionary specifies.
6. **Given** the user is comparing engines on licensing, **When** they inspect VoxCPM2, **Then** it is shown as permissively licensed and usable commercially.

---

### User Story 2 - Clone a voice with the new engine (Priority: P1)

A user who already has a Voice Profile — one reference clip or several — selects VoxCPM2 and generates in that voice. The result sounds like the person in the reference audio. Repeating the same generation with the same seed gives them the same audio again, so they can iterate on text without the voice drifting underneath them.

**Why this priority**: Cloning is the product's core capability, and an engine that cannot clone is a second-class citizen in this app. It is P1 alongside Story 1 because the licensing win in Story 1 is materially less useful if it only applies to generic voices.

**Independent Test**: Take an existing Voice Profile with one clip and another with several, generate with each under VoxCPM2, and confirm speaker likeness and seed reproducibility. Testable without any voice-design or availability work.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** a Voice Profile with a single reference clip, **When** the user generates with VoxCPM2, **Then** the output is recognisably the same speaker as the reference.
2. **Given** a Voice Profile with several reference clips, **When** the user generates with VoxCPM2, **Then** all of the clips inform the result and generation succeeds rather than failing or silently using only one.
3. **Given** the user has already generated once with a profile, **When** they generate again with that same profile, **Then** the second generation does not repeat the preparation work the first one already did.
4. **Given** the same text, voice and seed, **When** the user generates twice, **Then** the two results are identical.
5. **Given** the user has finished working with the engine, **When** they unload it, **Then** the memory it held is returned to the machine and the engine reports itself as not loaded.

---

### User Story 3 - Know up front whether this engine can run on this machine (Priority: P1)

A user on hardware that cannot run VoxCPM2 — the vendor documents no path outside a specific accelerator — never gets to pick it and then hit a wall. Either the engine is not offered at all, or it is offered greyed out with a plain sentence explaining why. They lose nothing and learn something; they do not download several gigabytes to discover the engine will not start.

**Why this priority**: P1 because the alternative is a user-visible crash on an entire class of machines, including every Mac if the vendor's constraint holds. The product's own rules require an engine to declare what it can run on and to report unavailability rather than fail at the point of use. A silent failure here is worse than not shipping the engine.

**Independent Test**: Run the app on hardware the engine does not support and confirm the engine is either absent from the picker or visibly disabled with a stated reason, and that no generation attempt reaches a crash. Testable without cloning or voice design.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** hardware that cannot run VoxCPM2, **When** the user opens the engine picker, **Then** the engine is either not listed or is listed as unavailable with a clear, specific reason.
2. **Given** hardware that cannot run VoxCPM2, **When** the user attempts to reach it by any route, **Then** they receive an explanatory refusal rather than an error, a hang, or a crash.
3. **Given** hardware that can run VoxCPM2, **When** the user opens the engine picker, **Then** the engine is offered normally with no warning.
4. **Given** the engine's hardware requirements, **When** any part of the product needs to know them, **Then** it reads them from the engine's own declaration rather than from a list that has to be kept in sync by hand.

---

### User Story 4 - Create a voice without having any recording (Priority: P3)

A user who wants a particular kind of voice but has nothing to clone from writes a short description of it — an age, a gender, a manner of speaking — and gets speech in a voice matching that description. This is the first way to make a custom voice in Voicebox without supplying audio.

**Why this priority**: P3 because it is genuinely new capability rather than parity, and the feature is coherent and shippable without it. It is the most likely thing to defer if the engine turns out to be harder to land than expected.

**Independent Test**: With no Voice Profile selected, supply a written voice description, generate, and confirm the voice audibly matches the description. Testable independently of cloning.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** no reference audio, **When** the user supplies a written description of a voice and generates, **Then** speech is produced in a voice matching that description.
2. **Given** a user who has only ever cloned voices, **When** they encounter this option, **Then** it is discoverable without reading documentation.

---

### Edge Cases

- A user starts the multi-gigabyte download and cancels it, loses connectivity, or quits the app part way through. The next attempt must resume or restart cleanly rather than leaving the engine permanently half-installed.
- A user selects VoxCPM2 while a different engine is loaded and the machine does not have room for both. The product must not leave the user with two partially loaded engines and no working generation.
- A user picks a language on another engine, then switches to VoxCPM2, and that language is not in this engine's list. The selection must resolve to something valid rather than silently generating in the wrong language.
- A Voice Profile was created with an engine that cannot clone. Selecting VoxCPM2 with that profile must behave predictably rather than producing an unrelated voice.
- The user's machine can technically run the engine but does not have enough memory for it in practice. [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: is "can run" a hard capability check only, or does it also account for insufficient memory on an otherwise supported accelerator? The two give different answers on a supported-but-small GPU.]
- A written voice description is supplied at the same time as a Voice Profile with reference audio. [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: which wins — the reference audio, the description, or is the combination rejected with an explanation?]
- Arabic text is supplied with a written voice description, where the description is in a different language than the text being spoken. [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: is a voice description in one language valid for speech in another, or must they match?]

## Requirements *(mandatory)*

### Functional Requirements

**Availability and selection**

- **FR-001**: The product MUST offer VoxCPM2 as a selectable speech engine wherever the existing engines are offered.
- **FR-002**: The product MUST declare, as part of the engine's own description, which hardware the engine can run on.
- **FR-003**: On hardware that cannot run the engine, the product MUST either withhold the engine from selection or present it as unavailable with a specific reason, and MUST NOT allow a user to reach a failed generation through it.
- **FR-004**: Any part of the product that needs the engine's hardware requirements or language coverage MUST obtain them from the engine's declaration rather than from a separately maintained list.
- **FR-005**: The product MUST present the engine's licence and its suitability for commercial use, as it does for the existing engines.

**Generation**

- **FR-006**: Users MUST be able to generate speech from text with this engine at its full 48 kHz output quality.
- **FR-007**: The product MUST offer exactly the languages this engine supports when it is selected, and that set MUST include Arabic.
- **FR-008**: Arabic generation MUST respect the existing pronunciation dictionary.
- **FR-009**: Given the same text, voice and seed, the product MUST produce the same audio every time.
- **FR-010**: The engine MUST use sensible, deliberately chosen defaults for its generation-quality settings rather than whatever the underlying library happens to default to. [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: should these settings also be exposed to users as advanced controls, or fixed at the chosen defaults for this release?]

**Voice cloning**

- **FR-011**: Users MUST be able to generate in a cloned voice from an existing Voice Profile with this engine.
- **FR-012**: The product MUST support Voice Profiles holding several reference clips with this engine, using all of them rather than an arbitrary one.
- **FR-013**: The product MUST avoid repeating reference-audio preparation work it has already done for the same profile.
- **FR-014**: The product MUST treat this engine as cloning-capable everywhere it distinguishes cloning engines from non-cloning ones.

**Voice design**

- **FR-015**: Users MUST be able to produce a voice from a written description without supplying any reference audio. [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: should this reuse the existing delivery-instruction input, or is a distinct "describe a voice" affordance required so users can tell the two apart?]

**Model lifecycle**

- **FR-016**: The product MUST show download progress for this engine's model, as it does for other engines.
- **FR-017**: Users MUST be able to unload the engine and recover the memory it was holding.
- **FR-018**: The product MUST report this engine's download size accurately so users can decide before committing to it. [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: the real size is not yet measured; the estimate in the source issue is approximate and must be confirmed before it is shown to users.]

**Installation and packaging**

- **FR-019**: Setting up the project from a clean checkout MUST succeed on both Windows and Linux with this engine included, without breaking the existing engines' dependencies.
- **FR-020**: The packaged desktop application MUST still build and start with this engine registered.

**Documentation**

- **FR-021**: The product's engine documentation and model-management documentation MUST cover this engine.
- **FR-022**: The user-visible addition MUST be recorded in the project changelog.

### Unresolved scope decisions

- **FR-023**: [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: does this engine run on ordinary processors at all, merely slowly, or is the specialised accelerator genuinely mandatory? If mandatory, this becomes the first engine in the product with no support on an entire platform, and FR-003's behaviour becomes the normal experience for those users rather than an edge case. The answer changes what Story 3 is worth and how it must be presented.]
- **FR-024**: [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: FR-004 requires capability to be declared once and read, but nothing in the product today carries engine capability from the engine to the interface — the interface keeps its own lists. Building that channel is work the source issue did not ask for. Confirm whether this feature builds it, or whether this engine is added to the existing hand-maintained lists and the divergence from the product's own rule is recorded instead.]

### Key Entities

- **Speech engine**: A named way of turning text into audio. Carries its own identity, display name, licence and commercial-use status, supported languages, download size, and — new with this feature — the hardware it can run on and whether it can clone.
- **Voice profile**: A user-created voice, holding one or more reference audio clips and their transcripts. Existing entity; this feature makes it usable with a new engine.
- **Voice description**: A short written description of a desired voice, used in place of reference audio. New with this feature.
- **Prepared voice reference**: The reusable result of processing a profile's reference audio for a particular engine, kept so the same work is not repeated.

## Success Criteria *(mandatory)*

### Measurable Outcomes

- **SC-001**: A user with a commercial use case can generate broad-dialect Arabic speech under a permissive licence, which is impossible today with any single option in the product.
- **SC-002**: A listener familiar with the reference speaker identifies a VoxCPM2-cloned generation as that speaker in at least 4 of 5 blind attempts.
- **SC-003**: 100% of repeat generations with an unchanged text, voice and seed produce identical audio.
- **SC-004**: On hardware that cannot run the engine, 0% of user attempts to use it end in a crash, a hang, or an unexplained error; every attempt ends in a stated reason.
- **SC-005**: A user who has never made a custom voice can produce one from a written description without consulting documentation.
- **SC-006**: A first-time user can tell how large the download is, and can see it progressing, before it completes.
- **SC-007**: Project setup from a clean checkout succeeds on both supported desktop platforms, and every engine that worked before this change still works after it.
- **SC-008**: The packaged desktop application still builds and starts.
- **SC-009**: Adding this engine required no new hand-maintained per-engine list in the user interface. *(Conditional on the resolution of FR-024.)*

## Assumptions

- The engine is added alongside the existing engines. Nothing that works today stops working, and no existing engine, model or voice is removed or replaced.
- Only one size of this model ships. Users are not asked to choose between variants of it, so none of the product's model-size machinery is involved.
- Streaming generation is not part of this feature; generation behaves like the product's other chunked engines.
- Reference audio, generated audio and model weights stay on the user's machine, as with every other engine. This feature introduces no new remote path.
- The existing consent and responsible-use affordances around voice cloning apply unchanged to this engine, including to voices created from a written description.
- The existing Voice Profile, pronunciation dictionary, download-progress and model-unload mechanisms are reused rather than rebuilt.
- Reproducibility (FR-009) is expected to hold for a given machine and engine version, not across different hardware or a future version of the model.
- "Recognisable speaker likeness" is judged by human listening, not by an automated similarity score, since the product ships no such score today.
- This repository is a fork that must stay cheaply mergeable with its upstream, so the change is expected to stay additive.
- The project's Python version floor is unchanged by this feature; changing it would require amending the constitution separately.
- The automated test suite for this area runs locally rather than in continuous integration, so verification of this feature is attested by the author at review time.

## Dependencies

- Availability of the third-party VoxCPM2 model and its distribution package, under the Apache-2.0 terms described in the source issue.
- The outcome of the dependency and platform probe that the source issue requires before implementation: it resolves FR-018 and FR-023, and informs FR-019.
- The existing pronunciation dictionary behaviour introduced in [PR #11](https://github.com/samykabu/voicebox/pull/11), which FR-008 depends on.

### C1Q1: If VoxCPM2 turns out to run only on NVIDIA graphics hardware, should it still ship?

@samykabu

**Why this matters:** It decides whether this feature is worth building as described. Every engine in Voicebox today works on every supported machine, falling back to the processor when there is no graphics acceleration. The people who publish this model document no such fallback. If that holds, this becomes the first engine that Mac users and AMD users simply cannot have, and the unavailable-engine experience stops being an edge case and becomes the normal experience for a large share of users.

- [ ] **D.** Do not ship it; close this issue and keep looking for a permissively licensed Arabic engine that runs everywhere
<!-- speckit-clarification:choices:end -->

**AI recommendation: A — Ship it on the hardware it supports, and make the unavailable state genuinely informative on everything else.**

**Why I recommend it:** The Arabic licensing problem is real today and has no other fix in the product, so an engine that helps some users is better than an engine that helps none. The project's fallback rule allows an engine to declare and enforce unsupported hardware rather than pretend to work, so this is a permitted exception rather than a violation, provided the unavailable state is honest. Waiting for a processor path that the model's authors have not promised risks waiting forever.

**Answer:** Tick one checkbox above, or add a normal comment: `C1Q1: A`. Nothing is selected for you.

### C1Q2: Should this feature build the missing channel that lets the backend tell the app what each engine can do, or add VoxCPM2 to the hand-maintained lists and record that we broke our own rule?

@samykabu

**Why this matters:** It changes the size and the risk of this work. The project's engineering rules say engine abilities must be declared once and then asked for, never written as per-engine special cases in the interface. Right now nothing carries that information: the app keeps its own hand-written list of engines and its own hand-written list of which languages each one speaks, and the backend's own list of engines is never sent anywhere. Adding VoxCPM2 the existing way means editing roughly eight interface files by hand, which is exactly what the rule forbids.

**Choose one:**

<!-- speckit-clarification:choices:start -->
- [x] **A.** Build the smallest real channel and use it for VoxCPM2 only **(Recommended)**
- [ ] **B.** Build the full channel and move all engines onto it now
- [ ] **C.** Add VoxCPM2 to the existing hand-maintained lists and record a deliberate exception to the rule
<!-- speckit-clarification:choices:end -->

**AI recommendation: A — Build the smallest real version of the channel: declare hardware support and languages on the engine, expose them, and have the app read them for this engine.**

**Why I recommend it:** The hardware requirement has nowhere to live otherwise, so some version of this is unavoidable rather than optional. Keeping it small means the seven existing engines are left alone, the change stays additive and easy to merge upstream, and the rule is honoured for the new engine without a product-wide refactor that this issue never asked for.

**Answer:** Tick one checkbox above, or add a normal comment: `C1Q2: A`. Nothing is selected for you.

**Optional feedback or another answer:** `C1Q2: your choice — your feedback`. You can answer several questions in one comment, one question ID per line. No Quote reply is needed.

<details>
<summary>More context</summary>

This matters more than usual here because this engine is the first one whose availability depends on the user's hardware. A hand-maintained list cannot express 'available on this machine but not that one', so the hardware requirement in particular has nowhere to live without some form of this channel. Building it properly also pulls in the project's contract rule: any new interface between backend and app must update the typed definitions, regenerate the client, and update the backend documentation in the same change. Doing the minimum instead means VoxCPM2 works but the next engine faces the same problem again, and this repository is a fork that has to stay easy to merge with its upstream, so a large architectural change carries its own cost.

</details>

### C1Q4: If a machine has the right kind of graphics hardware but not enough memory for the model, should the engine count as unavailable?

@samykabu

**Why this matters:** This is the most likely real-world failure and the specification does not cover it. VoxCPM2 is expected to be the heaviest engine in the product by a wide margin. A warning before the expensive step gives the user the information at the moment it is actionable, without the product pretending to know more than it does.

**Answer:** Tick one checkbox above, or add a normal comment: `C1Q4: B`. Nothing is selected for you.

<details>
<summary>More context</summary>

Treating it as unavailable is honest but needs a memory threshold that will be wrong for somebody, and available memory changes while the app is running depending on what else is open. Treating it as available means the user downloads several gigabytes before discovering the problem. A warning keeps the choice with the user but leaves them to judge something they may not understand. Note that whatever is chosen here also decides what happens when another engine is already loaded and holding memory.

</details>

### C1Q6: If someone supplies both a written voice description and a Voice Profile with reference audio, what should happen?

@samykabu

**Why this matters:** Both are ways of choosing a voice and they can contradict each other. Without a decision, whichever the code happens to check first silently wins, and the user gets a voice they did not ask for with no indication why.
